nameStory: The 'citrine' in this damselfly's name comes from the gemstone citrine, a pale yellow variety of quartz that matches the lovely lemon-yellow coloration found on parts of this delicate insect. The 'forktail' part refers to the distinctive forked appendages at the tip of the male's abdomen, which look like tiny prongs when viewed up close.
description: The Citrine Forktail is a small, slender damselfly that's one of our tiniest dragonfly relatives in New England. These delicate insects have narrow, clear wings that they hold vertically along their body when at rest, unlike dragonflies which spread their wings horizontally. Males typically display bright citrine-yellow and black coloration, while females can be more variable in color. They're quite small, usually measuring only about an inch and a quarter in length.

idTips.label: Forked tail appendages
idTips.description: Males have distinctive fork-shaped claspers at the tip of their abdomen that look like tiny black prongs - you'll need to look closely or use binoculars to see this key feature clearly

idTips.label: Citrine yellow coloration
idTips.description: Fresh males show bright lemon-yellow segments on their abdomen and thorax, creating a striking contrast against black markings

idTips.label: Wings held vertically
idTips.description: When perched, they fold their clear, narrow wings straight up along their back like a butterfly, rather than holding them out horizontally

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: One of our smallest damselflies - they're quite petite and delicate-looking, easily dwarfed by dragonflies and even some of the larger damselfly species

idTips.label: Weak flight pattern
idTips.description: Their flight appears fluttery and weak compared to dragonflies, often staying close to vegetation rather than making long, strong flights across open water

habitat: Look for Citrine Forktails around slow-moving or still freshwater areas like ponds, marshes, swamps, and the quiet backwaters of streams and rivers. They prefer areas with plenty of emergent vegetation like cattails, sedges, and water lilies where they can easily perch and find shelter. You'll often spot them resting on low vegetation near the water's edge, rarely venturing far from their aquatic breeding sites.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, typically May, as the water warms. Look for newly emerged individuals with very bright, fresh coloration near breeding waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs through summer months when you'll see them mating, laying eggs, and most actively flying. This is the best time for identification as populations are highest.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, though numbers decline. Late-season individuals may show more faded coloration but are still identifiable by their size and behavior.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with the first hard frosts, while eggs and larvae overwinter underwater in the mud and vegetation of ponds and slow streams.

funFact: Despite being called a 'forktail,' the distinctive forked appendages are only found on males and are actually specialized clasping organs used to grab females during mating - they're essentially the damselfly equivalent of hands designed specifically for romance!
confusionNotes: Citrine Forktails are easily confused with other small forktail damselflies, especially the Eastern Forktail and Fragile Forktail. The key is looking for that bright citrine-yellow coloration on males and always checking for the forked tail appendages with binoculars - other small damselflies have different-shaped tail structures.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'forktail' can be confusing because it specifically refers to the male's mating appendages, not the actual tail of the insect. Female forktails and immature males may lack the obvious forked structures, making identification more challenging and requiring attention to other features like size, color pattern, and habitat.
compareHints: Among New England's forktails, the Citrine Forktail is distinguished by its bright yellow coloration - Eastern Forktails tend to be more blue-green, while Fragile Forktails are typically orange. The Citrine is also generally smaller and more delicate-looking than the robust Eastern Forktail, and prefers more vegetated, swampy habitats compared to the Eastern's preference for more open waters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's forktails, Eastern Forktails are typically the most common and have the most pronounced fork marking at their tail tip.

Among New England's forktails, the Fragile Forktail's exclamation mark shoulder stripes set it apart from the Eastern Forktail's more linear shoulder markings and the Citrine Forktail's brighter yellow-green coloration.
Among New England's forktails, the Lilypad Forktail is most reliably identified by its strong association with floating vegetation and lily pads.
Among New England's forktails, Rambur's is distinguished by the male's two blue abdominal segments (8 and 9) versus the Eastern Forktail's single blue segment.
